=====================================================================
CR-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001
WorkBench Connectivity Posture — Bidirectional Integration as
Architectural Design Principle
Operator:       Dave Kitchens · Dropdown Logistics
Date:           2026-04-13
Classification: Architectural Stance — Cathedral Vision / Ratification
Distribution:   All Council Seats (1001–1010)
Mode:           Cathedral Vision + Ratification Candidate
                — NOT Synthesis, NOT Red Team
Format:         Pre-standardization draft, pattern candidate
Authored by:    Seat 1002 (Marcus Caldwell)
=====================================================================

CONTEXT

On the evening of 2026-04-12, during the design session for
WorkBench Module 1 (HR & People), the operator surfaced a
stance that reframes what WorkBench is in the market.

The operator said, mid-session: "I also want to be clear. I
want to be able to accept their data too."

That sentence — specifically the "too" — is doing more work
than its length suggests. Every SaaS product emits data
cleanly enough to be called "integration-compatible" in a
marketing deck. Far fewer are architected to ingest foreign
data losslessly, from first principles, from day one.

The operator's stance was more ambitious than outbound
connectivity. It was bidirectional connectivity as a design
principle governing every WorkBench module, every schema
decision, and every product-identity claim.

This review proposes CR-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001 as the architectural
stance and STD-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001 as the enforcement standard
that follows from it.

---

=====================================================================
THE THESIS
=====================================================================

Every WorkBench module is designed to accept external data,
not just emit it. Foreign systems — Gusto, BambooHR, QuickBooks,
Rippling, Xero, whatever the customer already runs — are
assumed as data sources from Module 1 onward, even when no
integrations ship in a given release.

The posture is not "we will build integrations eventually."
The posture is "we will never ship a design decision that
makes integration harder than it needs to be."

This inverts the standard SaaS commercial pitch. Most
platforms tell the customer to migrate to them. WorkBench
tells the customer to bring what they have. WorkBench makes
it work with everything else.

Bring Your Data is not a feature. It is a stance that shapes
every schema choice, every enum definition, every identifier
convention, every timestamp handling decision, across every
module WorkBench will ever ship.

=====================================================================
WHAT THE STANCE DEMANDS
=====================================================================

The stance translates into two classes of requirements:
hard (must be baked in from day one because retrofit is
prohibitively expensive) and soft (good hygiene, addable
later via simple migrations).

-----
HARD REQUIREMENTS — NON-NEGOTIABLE FROM DAY ONE
-----

REQ-1 — IMMUTABLE FACT TABLES
Event-driven schemas where changes are append-only rows, not
overwrites. External systems syncing with WorkBench need to
reason about "what happened when." Overwrite semantics
destroy that reasoning. Non-retrofittable.

REQ-2 — STABLE EXTERNAL-SAFE IDENTIFIERS
Namespaced, human-readable, stable IDs (EMP-###, CTL-###,
CLI-###). No auto-incrementing integers exposed as canonical
keys. External systems map against these IDs. Once assigned,
never change. Non-retrofittable.

REQ-3 — UTC TIMESTAMPS
Every stored timestamp in UTC. Localization is a rendering
concern. External systems cannot reliably sync against
timestamps whose timezone is ambiguous. Non-retrofittable.

REQ-4 — CANONICAL ENUM VOCABULARIES
Status values, event types, role taxonomies — all in lookup
tables with disciplined vocabularies. Free-text status fields
become integration nightmares as every sync requires fuzzy
matching. Canonical vocabularies make external mapping
possible. Non-retrofittable in practice (retrofit = data
cleanup at customer scale).

-----
SOFT REQUIREMENTS — ADDABLE LATER WITHOUT PAIN
-----

SOFT-1 — EXTERNAL ID FIELDS
Every dimension table eventually carries an externalId field
holding the foreign system's identifier for the record. Can
be added via ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN. Module 1 does not need
to implement; the architecture must not fight it.

SOFT-2 — EXTERNAL METADATA PRESERVATION
Foreign systems carry fields WorkBench does not model. Those
fields are preserved in externalMetadata (JSONB), never
dropped. If WorkBench later adds a native field for a
preserved attribute, data migrates from metadata to the
proper column. Ingestion is lossless.

SOFT-3 — SOURCE TRACKING
Every fact row eventually carries source (internal / import /
sync_<system>) and sourceRecordId (foreign system's event ID).
Enables deduplication and bidirectional reconciliation.
Module 1 does not need to implement.

SOFT-4 — IMPORT BATCH INFRASTRUCTURE
Bulk imports generate ImportBatch rows with metadata (who,
when, source, record count, mapping rules). Every event from
that batch references the batch ID. Enables "undo this
import" and batch-scoped queries. Module 1 does not need to
implement; table name is reserved in the namespace.

-----
THE DISCIPLINE OF THE GUIDING QUESTION
-----

Every design decision in every WorkBench module gets weighed
with one question:

    "Does this choice make bidirectional connectivity easier
    or harder later?"

If harder, reconsider. If neutral, ship the simpler version.
If easier, prefer.

This is not a schema audit checklist. It is a stance applied
per decision, at the moment of decision.

---

=====================================================================
THE INBOUND DIRECTION — WHY IT'S THE HARDER HALF
=====================================================================

Outbound connectivity is a posture most products claim.
Inbound connectivity is a posture few products actually
deliver.

The asymmetry comes from what each direction requires:

OUTBOUND — emit data
  We control the schema.
  We control the format.
  We control the completeness.
  The consumer handles the mapping.
er.

The asymmetry comes from what each direction requires:

OUTBOUND — emit data
  We control the schema.
  We control the format.
  We control the completeness.
  The consumer handles the mapping.

INBOUND — accept data
  We accept whatever shape the source sent.
  We transform without losing fidelity.
  We arbitrate conflicts with existing records.
  We preserve unmapped attributes.
  We handle idempotency under repeated imports.

Inbound connectivity requires decisions that outbound never
forces: conflict resolution rules, source-of-truth arbitration,
lossless preservation of unmodeled fields, mapping convention
documentation, idempotency at scale.

None of those decisions need to be made in Module 1.
All of them must be makeable later without restructuring
Module 1's foundations.

---

=====================================================================
WHAT THE STANCE DOES NOT MEAN
=====================================================================

The Bring Your Data stance is widely misinterpretable.
Explicit non-commitments:

NOT — "WorkBench ships with integrations on day one"
    Connectivity is a posture, not a feature. Integrations
    arrive when they arrive, via the Integrations module
    or via customer-specific work.

NOT — "WorkBench accepts any data format from any source"
    Ingestion requires a mapping layer. The stance commits
    to making mapping possible and clean, not to accepting
    arbitrary formats unattended.

NOT — "Every module ships with import tooling"
    Import UIs are module-scoped feature work. The stance
    ensures schemas are import-ready when import UIs are built.

NOT — "Customer data is trusted on ingestion"
    Validation, conflict resolution, and source-of-truth
    arbitration still apply. The stance does not remove
    governance; it ensures governance is possible.

    Validation, conflict resolution, and source-of-truth
    arbitration still apply. The stance does not remove
    governance; it ensures governance is possible.

NOT — "Connectivity-compatible is a marketing claim today"
    Promotion follows capability. We do not claim
    Gusto-compatibility in marketing until we have shipped
    and tested a Gusto sync. The stance is internal
    discipline; external claims require demonstrated
    capability.

=====================================================================
THE TARGET PLATFORM RESEARCH LIST
=====================================================================

Platforms WorkBench should study — not to integrate with
yet, but to understand the shape of data WorkBench will
eventually need to accept:

HR & People
  BambooHR, Namely, Zenefits, Rippling, Workday (enterprise)

Payroll
  Gusto, Rippling, ADP, QuickBooks Payroll, Paychex

Time Tracking
  Harvest, Toggl, Clockify, TimeDoctor

Accounting
  QuickBooks, Xero, NetSuite, FreshBooks

CRM
  Salesforce, HubSpot, Pipedrive, Close

SSO / Identity
  Okta, Google Workspace, Microsoft Entra, Auth0

File & Document
  Google Drive, Dropbox, OneDrive, Box

Benefits
  Sequoia, TriNet, Justworks

Each of these systems has schema conventions, ID formats,
timestamp handling, and enum vocabularies that differ from
each other and from what WorkBench will author. Studying
their shapes informs what WorkBench's ingestion layer must
accommodate.

This research list is not ratified here. It is surfaced as
the scope of CR-WB-PITFALLS-001 (the research review
currently in queue) and as the platform set against which
STD-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001's import specification will be
tested.

=====================================================================
VERDICT FORMAT
=====================================================================

Per-stance verdicts:
  RATIFY_STANCE — Accept Bring Your Data as architectural
                  principle governing all future WorkBench
                  modules.
  RATIFY_STANCE_REVISE — Accept the stance, revise wording
                         or scope.
  REFRAME — The stance is real but named wrong; propose
            alternative framing.
  REJECT_STANCE — Connectivity should not be a foundational
                  stance; argue for treating it as a feature
                  instead.

Per-requirement verdicts:
  RATIFY — Requirement stands as written.
  RECLASSIFY — Move requirement between hard and soft lists.
  SPLIT — One requirement should be two.
  MERGE — Collapse into another requirement.
  ADD — New requirement missing from the draft.

=====================================================================
ONE CLOSING OBSERVATION
=====================================================================

The operator's framing — "I want to be able to accept their
data too" — is a one-sentence commercial strategy disguised
as a technical preference. Every competitor in the modular
business OS category is optimized for customer migration
into their platform. Few are optimized for customer continuity
from their existing platforms.

The stance turns WorkBench into the infrastructure layer
that accepts the messy reality of a customer's existing
stack and makes sense of it, rather than asking the customer
to abandon what they have and adopt something new.

This is not how most SaaS platforms position themselves.
The ones that do — and do it credibly — tend to win the
operators they court, because the operator's first question
is always "what happens to my existing data," and the
standard SaaS answer is "we'll migrate it" (meaning: you
will lose things you didn't know mattered until they're gone).

Bring Your Data inverts that first question. The operator's
existing data is not a migration problem. It is the seed
data for WorkBench.

### **STANCE VERDICT**
**RATIFY_STANCE**
*"Bring Your Data"* is **architecturally sound** and **commercially transformative**. It inverts the SaaS migration narrative from *"abandon your stack"* to *"augment your stack"*, which is a **defensible differentiator** in the modular business OS market.

**Commercial Translation:**
- **Public-facing thesis:** *"Your Data, Your Way"* or *"No Forced Migrations"*
- **Value proposition:** *"WorkBench works with what you have—no data loss, no lock-in, no disruption."*
- **Competitive framing:**
  - **Vs. Rippling/Gusto:** *"They ask you to migrate to their platform. We ask you to bring your data to ours."*
  - **Vs. Custom builds:** *"They require you to build integrations. We’re built to accept your data from day one."*

### **COMMERCIAL IMPLICATIONS (SEAT 1001 DEEP DIVE)**

#### **1. Market Positioning**
- **Category:** WorkBench is **not** competing with Rippling/Gusto on features. It’s competing on **data philosophy**.
- **Unique Value Prop:** *"The only business OS designed to accept your existing data as a first-class citizen."*
- **Target Audience:** SMBs with **heterogeneous stacks** (e.g., Gusto for payroll + QuickBooks for accounting + Slack for comms). These businesses are **underserved** by "all-in-one" platforms that force migration.

#### **2. Messaging Framework**
| **Internal Term**       | **Customer-Facing Language**       | **Why It Works**                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------|
| Bring Your Data         | "Your Data, Your Way"               | Simple, emotional, benefit-focused.      |
| Bidirectional Connectivity | "Works With What You Have"       | Addresses fear of disruption.           |
| Immutable Fact Tables   | "Complete, Tamper-Proof History"    | Trust-building for audits/compliance.   |
| Canonical Enum Vocabs   | "Consistent Data, Everywhere"      | Highlights reliability.                  |

#### **3. Competitive Moat**
- **Barrier to Entry:** Most SaaS platforms **cannot** retroactively adopt this stance. Their schemas are already hardcoded, their IDs are auto-incrementing, their timestamps are localized.
- **Lock-In Resistance:** WorkBench’s stance **reduces** customer lock-in (they can export their data + WorkBench accepts external data). This is counterintuitive for SaaS but **strategically powerful** for trust.

#### **4. Risk Mitigation**
- **Expectation Management:** Clearly distinguish between:
  - **Stance:** "We’re built to accept your data." (Always true)
  - **Feature:** "We integrate with [Gusto/BambooHR]." (Only true when shipped)
- **Avoid:** Claiming "Bring Your Data" means "zero setup." It means **"zero structural barriers"**—there’s still mapping, validation, and potential manual work.

### **SYNTHESIS NOTES**

1. **Architectural Coherence:**
   - The hard requirements **perfectly align** with STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001 (immutable facts, stable IDs, UTC timestamps, lookup tables).
   - **SOFT-2 → HARD** is the only critical adjustment. Lossless ingestion is the **litmus test** of the stance.

2. **iPaaS Coexistence (for Grey):**
   - WorkBench **coexists** with Zapier/Make/n8n. It doesn’t replace them.
   - **WorkBench’s role:** The **data substrate** that integration tools can reliably sync with (thanks to stable IDs, UTC timestamps, etc.).
   - **Integration tools’ role:** The **pipes** that move data between WorkBench and other systems.

3. **AuditForge Synergy (Q5):**
   - AuditForge is the **proof of concept** for this stance. Its architecture already embodies the hard requirements.
   - **Opportunity:** Use AuditForge as the **reference implementation** for WorkBench modules.

4. **Engineering Pragmatism (for Rowan):**
   - **SOFT-2 (now HARD)** is the most at-risk requirement. Engineers may be tempted to drop "unimportant" fields during ingestion.
   - **Enforcement:** Automated tests that verify `externalMetadata` captures all unmapped source fields.

**THE HARD/SOFT SPLIT — IS IT CORRECTLY DRAWN?**

Three hard requirements are correctly hard. One is nearly hard. Two soft requirements are secretly hard. Details below.

**REQ-1 (Immutable fact tables)** — correctly hard. Retrofit requires rewriting every module that used overwrite semantics. Non-negotiable. Keep.

**REQ-2 (Stable external-safe IDs)** — correctly hard. Swapping ID conventions after integrations exist breaks every integration. Non-negotiable. Keep.

**REQ-3 (UTC timestamps)** — correctly hard. Retrofitting timezone-ambiguous timestamps at customer scale is a nightmare. Keep.

**REQ-4 (Canonical enum vocabularies)** — correctly hard, but the weakest of the four. A module author can ship free-text status fields and claim conformance because the standard's enforcement surface is blurry. Kai's prompt is exactly right to flag this. The fix is in Requirement 8 of STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001 (categories as lookup tables), which operationalizes this requirement at the schema level. Cross-reference the two documents explicitly. Don't soften this requirement — harden it by pointing at the fact-layer enforcement.

**SOFT-1 (External ID fields)** — correctly soft. Adding `externalId` columns via ALTER TABLE is trivial. Deferring to when actually needed is fine.

**SOFT-2 (External metadata preservation)** — **secretly hard.** Rowan's prompt nails this. Dropping fields during ingestion is the failure mode most likely to happen silently. By the time a customer notices their BambooHR custom field didn't come through, the import has run, the data is stale at the source, and reconstruction requires re-running the entire sync. The fix isn't to harden SOFT-2 itself — it's to specify that whenever an import flow ships for any module, that flow must implement lossless metadata preservation from the first version. The requirement stays soft for schema design. It becomes hard the moment import tooling ships. That gating should be explicit in the standard.

**SOFT-3 (Source tracking)** — correctly soft. The `source` and `sourceRecordId` columns can be added later without data loss. Deferring is fine.

**SOFT-4 (Import batch infrastructure)** — **secretly hard in one specific way.** The table name `ImportBatch` being reserved in the namespace is fine as a soft requirement. But: the `fact` table schemas need to accommodate a future `importBatchId` foreign key from day one. That means fact tables should have room in their indexing strategy for an import-batch-scoped query path. This isn't a required column on day one. It's a required consideration for how fact tables are indexed and partitioned. Worth flagging in the standard as a note rather than elevating to hard.

**Missing from the requirements list entirely:** idempotency handling for repeated imports. A customer re-running the same BambooHR sync twice should not produce duplicate fact rows. This requires either a deduplication key on import events or a sourceRecordId uniqueness constraint scoped by source. It's related to SOFT-3 but architecturally distinct. Recommend adding as SOFT-5 or folding into an expanded SOFT-3.

The stance is correct: WorkBench should be designed to accept external data as a first-class posture, not as a retrofit. That is a differentiator, not just a feature.  

The draft is also correctly warning against false promises: “Bring Your Data” should remain an internal design stance until actual import paths exist and have been tested. ## 1) Hard vs soft split

**Verdict: RECLASSIFY some items, RATIFY the rest.**  

### Keep hard
- Immutable fact tables.
- Stable external-safe identifiers.
- UTC timestamps.
- Canonical enum vocabularies.

Those are properly day-one, non-retrofittable foundations.

### Move to hard
- **External metadata preservation** should be treated as hard in spirit, even if the mechanism is soft. If you allow silent dropping of unmapped fields, you’ve broken the stance. The storage field can be added later, but the requirement to preserve unmapped inbound data should be hard.
- **Source tracking** should also be hard in principle for any actual import or sync path. Even if Module 1 ships before import UI, the schema should reserve the shape and the rule should be explicit.

## 2) Conflict resolution

**Verdict: ADD.**  
Yes, CR-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001 should explicitly require a conflict resolution and source-of-truth arbitration framework, but the full logic can live in a follow-on standard.  

I would add a hard requirement like this:  
> Every inbound integration path must define source-of-truth rules, deduplication behavior, idempotency handling, and conflict resolution outcomes before data is accepted into the fact layer.  

That keeps the stance honest. If you accept foreign data, you must declare how conflicts resolve or you are not really bidirectional — you are just ingesting with hope.

***

## 3) Marketing discipline

**Verdict: RATIFY with caution.**  
“Promotion follows capability” is the correct operating rule. The stance itself is marketable as philosophy, but it should not be marketed as a delivered integration capability until actual import workflows exist and have been tested.  

So the distinction is:
- **Marketable now:** “Bring Your Data” as a product philosophy.
- **Not marketable yet:** named compatibility claims with specific systems.

That protects trust and keeps the claim aligned with reality.

The draft currently presents the list as an appendix to the stance. That is fine, as long as it is clear that the stance does not require researching every platform before shipping Module 1.

-----
CANDIDATE 1 — BlueprintInversion
-----
Type:       Failure mode
Proposed by: PM thread, 2026-04-12

DEFINITION
The anti-pattern of constructing before planning. Architecture
discovered after the structure is already built, usually by
running into its limits. Distinct from "cottage to cathedral"
(scope creep) — this describes specifically the inversion of
the natural build order: cathedral first, plans later.

PROVENANCE
Operator MDN mid-session: "Planning before building is
somewhat novel, or just that it's not necessarily default.
This is in the 'cottage to cathedral' vein but that's about
scope creep. This is more about building the cathedral and
then drawing up plans."

Industry default is BlueprintInversion. Ship first, plan
retroactively, discover the load-bearing walls are in the
wrong places, retrofit at 10x the original cost.

-----

CR-WB-FACTLAYER-001
WorkBench Fact Layer Governance Standard — Foundational
Architecture for Cross-Module Event-Driven Data
Operator:       Dave Kitchens · Dropdown Logistics
Date:           2026-04-13
Classification: Architectural Standard — Cathedral Vision / Ratification
Distribution:   All Council Seats (1001–1010)
Mode:           Cathedral Vision + Ratification Candidate
                — NOT Synthesis, NOT Red Team
Format:         Pre-standardization draft, pattern candidate
Authored by:    Seat 1002 (Marcus Caldwell)
=====================================================================

CONTEXT

On the evening of 2026-04-12, during the design session for
WorkBench Module 1 (HR & People), the operator and PM thread
arrived at what is arguably the most load-bearing architectural
commitment WorkBench can make: every module writes events to
the same governed fact layer, enabling native cross-module
queries without integration work.

This is not a Module 1 decision. It is the decision that
determines what WorkBench becomes as it grows beyond Module 1.

Get this right, and WorkBench's "Everything, Everywhere, All
At Once" thesis (CR-WB-CANON-001, Candidate 3) has structural
backing. The value proposition compounds per module: each new
module adds to every existing analytics view automatically
because they share substrate.

Get this wrong, and WorkBench becomes another modular SaaS
pitching bundled convenience, with separate schemas that
require sync jobs and ETL pipelines to reconcile.

This review proposes STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001 as the foundational
architectural standard every WorkBench module must conform to.
The standard is load-bearing for STD-WB-MODULE-001 (the
module standard, CR-WB-MODULE-001) and for the analytics
roadmap (CR-WB-ANALYTICS-001).

=====================================================================
THE THESIS
=====================================================================

Every module in WorkBench writes immutable events to a
governed fact layer. All events across all modules share a
key contract. Category-scoped fact tables plus a master event
log together form one logical queryable substrate, physically
separated for schema fit, logically unified for cross-module
access.

The industry default is the opposite. Each product in a
"suite" has its own schema, its own event semantics, its own
timestamp conventions, its own identifiers. Cross-product
queries require integration layers, ETL pipelines, or data
warehouses built after the fact. WorkBench's architectural
advantage is declining to separate in the first place.

---

=====================================================================
THE STANDARD — WHAT EVERY WORKBENCH MODULE MUST DO
=====================================================================

The following requirements apply to every module shipped in
WorkBench, without exception. A module that violates any of
these cannot ship.

-----
REQUIREMENT 1 — EVENT-DRIVEN, IMMUTABLE FACT TABLES
-----

Every change to a dimension-table attribute creates an
immutable row in a fact table. Dimension tables reflect
current state. Fact tables reflect history. Dimension
updates happen by writing a new fact row and updating the
dimension pointer, never by overwriting the dimension.

No module may use overwrite semantics on fields that change
over time. Status flips, role changes, title updates,
department moves, rehires — all are events, all are immutable,
all are queryable historically.

over time. Status flips, role changes, title updates,
department moves, rehires — all are events, all are immutable,
all are queryable historically.

The rehire case is the canonical proof. An employee
transitions active → inactive → active. Same employee ID.
Three fact rows. No nullable termination-date fields. No
ambiguity about whether this is their first or second stint.
The fact table tells the story.

Rationale: bitemporal reconstruction, audit-grade trails,
and cross-module analytics all require immutable facts.
Retrofit is a full rewrite.

-----
REQUIREMENT 2 — SHARED KEY CONTRACT
-----

Every fact table in every module must include the following
fields at minimum:

  entityId         — FK to the dimension being tracked
  eventId          — unique identifier for this event row
  eventType        — FK to Dim_EventType (lookup table,
                     per Requirement 8)
  fieldChanged     — the dimension attribute this event
                     modified
  previousValue    — JSONB, the value before the change
  newValue         — JSONB, the value after the change
  effectiveDate    — TIMESTAMPTZ, UTC, when the change
                     applies in business reality
  recordedDate     — TIMESTAMPTZ, UTC, when the change
                     was entered into the system
  recordedBy       — FK to user/operator who recorded it
  source           — enum: internal / import / sync_<system>
  transactionId    — groups related events from one
                     logical change (e.g., a promotion
                     that changes role + title + pay +
                     manager in one transaction)
  reason           — optional free text

Modules may add fields specific to their domain. Modules
may not remove or rename contract fields.

Rationale: the key contract is what makes GovernedCohesion
(CR-WB-CANON-001, Candidate 5) possible. Without it,
cross-module queries become integration problems.

-----
REQUIREMENT 3 — CATEGORY-SCOPED FACT TABLES + MASTER EVENT LOG
-----

Each module maintains category-specific fact tables for
distinct event domains. HR & People has Fact_StatusChange,
Fact_RoleChange, Fact_CompensationChange, Fact_TokenScoreChange,
etc. Each table has schema fit for its category.

Every module additionally writes a thin record to a unified
master event log (Fact_EventLog or per-module equivalent)
containing:

  eventId          — matches the category-table row
  entityId
  eventType
  effectiveDate
  recordedDate
  sourceTable      — which category table holds the detail
  sourceRowId      — FK to the detail row

The master event log answers "show me everything that
happened to entity X" without UNION ALL across all category
tables. Category tables answer "show me all events of type Y
with full detail."

Rationale: pure category-scoped without a master log makes
timeline queries painful. Pure monolithic without category
scope makes schema polymorphism messy. Both together is the
architecturally disciplined answer.

-----
REQUIREMENT 4 — BITEMPORAL TIMESTAMPS
-----

Every fact row carries both effectiveDate and recordedDate.
In the common case they match (normal edits populate both
with NOW() at write time). When backdating, they diverge.

Bitemporality is not optional. It is the mechanism by which
WorkBench answers "what did the system believe on date X"
vs "what was true on date X." These are distinct questions.
Accounting needs it. Audit needs it. Compliance needs it.
HR needs it more often than it looks (backdated terminations,
retroactive pay changes).

Storage cost: 8 bytes per row. Option cost of not having it:
massive.

-----
REQUIREMENT 5 — UTC TIMESTAMPS, NO EXCEPTIONS
-----

retroactive pay changes).

Storage cost: 8 bytes per row. Option cost of not having it:
massive.

-----
REQUIREMENT 5 — UTC TIMESTAMPS, NO EXCEPTIONS
-----

Every timestamp in every module's schema is stored in UTC.
Local time is a rendering concern, not a storage concern.

Modules that need to surface "when was this event local to
the user" compute it at query/render time from the user's
timezone setting, never store localized timestamps.

Rationale: timezone ambiguity in stored timestamps is a
retrofit nightmare. Cross-timezone queries become impossible
when timestamps are "local to whoever wrote the row."

-----
REQUIREMENT 6 — STABLE EXTERNAL-SAFE IDENTIFIERS
-----

Every dimension record uses a human-readable, stable,
external-safe identifier. Pattern: three-letter domain prefix
followed by a sequence number (EMP-001, CTL-001, CLI-001,
PRJ-001). Auto-incrementing integers are not exposed as
canonical keys.

Once assigned, an entity's ID never changes. Rehires,
renames, mergers, transfers — all preserve the original ID.
External systems synchronizing with WorkBench can map
against these IDs without worrying about them shifting.

Rationale: stable IDs are the integration substrate. Swapping
auto-incrementing integers for namespaced IDs later breaks
every integration anyone built on them.

-----
REQUIREMENT 7 — TYPED VALUES VIA JSONB
-----

The previousValue and newValue fields on fact rows are
JSONB, not strings. Types are preserved natively — integers
as integers, dates as dates, nested objects as objects.

Queries against specific value types are possible via
PostgreSQL JSONB operators. Aggregate queries that need
typed numeric operations cast at query time.

Rationale: stringifying everything loses type signal and
complicates analytics. JSONB is Postgres-native, performant,
and preserves structure for compound-value events.

-----
REQUIREMENT 8 — CATEGORIES AS LOOKUP TABLES
-----

complicates analytics. JSONB is Postgres-native, performant,
and preserves structure for compound-value events.

-----
REQUIREMENT 8 — CATEGORIES AS LOOKUP TABLES
-----

Per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 6 (AllCategoriesExpand), every
categorical attribute lives in a lookup table, not a database
enum. Status values, event types, roles, departments, token
categories — all are Dim_* lookup tables with rows that can
grow.

Required fields on every category lookup table:

  categoryId         — stable external-safe ID
  parentCategoryId   — self-referential FK for hierarchical
                       taxonomies
  name               — canonical label
  displayName        — may differ from name for UI
  effectiveDate      — when this category became available
  deprecatedDate     — nullable; when this category stopped
                       being available (never delete rows)
  flags              — JSONB; behavioral attributes that
                       drive business logic (e.g.,
                       rehire_eligible: true,
                       counts_as_headcount: false)
  scope              — enum: universal / role_specific /
                       customer_custom / system
  metadata           — JSONB for attributes not yet modeled

Rationale: hardcoded enums are retrofits waiting to happen.
Every category in DDL history has wanted to expand at some
point.

-----
REQUIREMENT 9 — CONNECTIVITY-COMPATIBLE SCHEMA
-----

Per CR-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001 and the "Bring Your Data"
stance (CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 4): every dimension
table is designed such that external ID, external metadata,
and source tracking fields can be added via simple
ALTER TABLE migrations without structural rework.

This does not mean Module 1 implements these fields. It
means Module 1 does not ship schema choices that would
require restructuring when these fields arrive.

Specifically, Module 1 must:
  — Use nullable fields where external systems might

  — Avoid hardcoded application logic tied to field presence
  — Design foreign keys to tolerate imported data without

-----
REQUIREMENT 10 — LEDGER-EXPORTABLE FLAGS
-----

Per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 10 (PortableRecord): every
field on every dimension and every token carries a
ledger_exportable boolean flag. Module 1 does not use the
flag. The Ledger export module (future) reads it and builds
export manifests from it.

Modules propose which of their fields are appropriate for
Ledger export. The operator ratifies per module. No field
is Ledger-exported without explicit opt-in.

-----
REQUIREMENT 11 — RELATIONALRENDERING METADATA
-----

Per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 8 (RelationalRendering):
every field on every dimension and every token carries
visibility and editability metadata for each viewer-relationship
class. Module 1 may expose limited viewer classes (operator-only,
for example), but the metadata columns exist from day one so
later modules can extend viewer classes without retrofitting
every table.

Minimum viewer classes: self, direct_manager, management_chain,
backoffice, operator, peer (future).

For each class: visible (boolean), editable (boolean).

-----
REQUIREMENT 12 — GOVERNANCE IS LOAD-BEARING, NOT ADVISORY
-----

STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001 is a hard gate. Modules that violate
any requirement above cannot ship. There is no "ship it
now and fix later." Retrofit is too expensive on these
specific fields.

### **COMMERCIAL IMPLICATIONS (SEAT 1001 FOCUS)**

#### **1. Marketing Claim: "Every Module Conforms to This Standard"**
- **Strength:** This is a **unique, defensible differentiator**. Competitors (Rippling, Gusto) pitch "modular" but require ETL/integration for cross-module queries. WorkBench’s **native cross-module access** is a **category-defining advantage**.
- **Translation for Customers:**
  - *"No integration headaches. Every WorkBench module shares the same data foundation."*
  - *"Your analytics work across all modules, out of the box."*
  - *"Complete audit history, without retrofits."*

Fact tables should remain append-only, but dimension tables need explicit soft-delete semantics or status-deprecation semantics.

## SPECIFIC QUESTIONS (OPERATOR’S FIVE)

**1. RelationalRendering metadata (Req 11) — fact layer or separate access standard?**

**Fact layer, but with a critical refinement.** The metadata belongs here because rendering is a function of the viewer’s relationship to the *record*, which is intrinsic to the record’s governance, not an external policy. However, the standard should specify that visibility/editing rules are *evaluated at query time* against the viewer’s role, not stored per viewer. The proposed `visible`/`editable` flags per viewer class are a good start, but they risk becoming a matrix that scales poorly as viewer classes grow. **Recommendation:** Replace per‑class boolean flags with a single `visibility_policy` JSONB field that maps viewer class to a rule expression (e.g., `{"self": true, "manager": "if department matches", "backoffice": false}`). This is more flexible and still enforceable.

**2. Ledger‑exportable flags (Req 10) — fact layer or Ledger standard?**
g., `{"self": true, "manager": "if department matches", "backoffice": false}`). This is more flexible and still enforceable.

**2. Ledger‑exportable flags (Req 10) — fact layer or Ledger standard?**

**Fact layer, but as a forward‑declared pointer, not an implementation.** The flag belongs here because it is a property of the field itself (is this field part of the portable record?), not a Ledger implementation detail. The standard should specify that the `ledger_exportable` flag is a boolean that the Ledger module reads, but the Ledger module is responsible for export mechanics. This is correctly placed.

**3. Soft‑delete as Requirement 13?**  
**Yes.** The standard implies append‑only facts, but dimension tables need soft‑delete. Add Requirement 13: “Soft‑delete semantics for dimension records. Dimensions must have `valid_to` (nullable) and `is_current` boolean. Deletion is achieved by setting `valid_to` to now() and `is_current` to false. Hard deletes are forbidden. Fact tables are append‑only, never soft‑deleted.”

**4. Retention and GDPR as Requirement 14?**  
**No. Retention is a separate standard.** Immutable facts are load‑bearing for audit and analytics. GDPR deletion requests cannot be satisfied by deleting rows without breaking that substrate. The solution is to store a `deletion_requested` flag and a `deletion_token` that, when present, causes the record to be excluded from queries (but retained for internal audit). This is complex enough to warrant its own standard: `STD-WB-RETENTION-001`. The fact layer standard should simply note that retention is handled elsewhere and that fact tables are immutable by design.

**5. “Cannot ship” too strict? Conditional approval?**

**Does the key contract hold under edge cases?**  
- **Bulk imports with thousands of events sharing a single `transactionId`** – Yes, as long as the import is atomic (Req 15). The `transactionId` is a grouping key, not a unit of atomicity. The database transaction provides atomicity.  
- **Cascading deletions** – Not applicable. Fact tables are append‑only. Dimensions are soft‑deleted (Req 13). No cascade.

CR-WB-MODULE-001
WorkBench Module Standard — Structural Requirements Every
Module Must Satisfy to Ship
Operator:       Dave Kitchens · Dropdown Logistics
Date:           2026-04-13
Classification: Product Standard — Cathedral Vision / Ratification
Distribution:   All Council Seats (1001–1010)

Format:         Pre-standardization draft, pattern candidate

CONTEXT

WorkBench is a modular business OS. Seventeen modules exist
conceptually on the promo page. One (HR & People) is in
active specification. Sixteen remain to be designed and
built over the coming months and years.

Without a module standard, each module risks being designed
in isolation, with its own conventions for schemas, measures,
visibility, connectivity, and analytics. The "Everything,
Everywhere, All At Once" thesis fails the moment two modules
ship with incompatible event semantics. The "Bring Your Data"
stance fails the moment a module ships with schema choices
that fight inbound ingestion.

This review proposes STD-WB-MODULE-001 — the standard every
WorkBench module must conform to in order to ship. The
standard composes earlier standards (fact layer, connectivity,
analytics) and adds module-level requirements that emerge
from coherence across the set.

STD-WB-MODULE-001 is the reference against which every future
module is checked. CR-WB-HRPEOPLE-001 (CR-1) treats HR & People
as the first reference implementation.

=====================================================================
THE THESIS
=====================================================================

A WorkBench module is not defined by what it does. It is
defined by what it writes, how it writes it, and what promises
it makes to the rest of the system.

The module standard governs the promises. A module that
conforms ships. A module that violates any requirement returns
to design. This is not advisory. This is a hard gate, because
the economics of a modular platform collapse the moment any
single module breaks the substrate.

---

=====================================================================
WHAT EVERY WORKBENCH MODULE MUST DO
=====================================================================

Twelve structural requirements, organized into four categories:
Foundation, Data Model, Interface, and Governance.

-----
CATEGORY A — FOUNDATION (WHAT THE MODULE SITS ON)
-----

REQ-A1 — FACT LAYER CONFORMANCE
The module writes all state changes as events to
category-scoped fact tables plus the master event log, per
STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001. No exceptions. Dimension tables reflect
current state; fact tables reflect history. Overwrite
semantics on any field that changes over time is a ship
blocker.

REQ-A2 — CONNECTIVITY CONFORMANCE
The module's schema satisfies the hard requirements of
STD-WB-CONNECTIVITY-001 from day one: immutable fact tables,
stable external-safe IDs, UTC timestamps, canonical enum
vocabularies via lookup tables. Soft requirements (externalId
fields, externalMetadata preservation, source tracking, import
batch infrastructure) may be deferred but the schema must not
fight them.
vocabularies via lookup tables. Soft requirements (externalId
fields, externalMetadata preservation, source tracking, import
batch infrastructure) may be deferred but the schema must not
fight them.

REQ-A3 — MEASURE LAYER REGISTRATION
Every chart, statistic, or queryable number the module
surfaces to customers must be declared as a measure in the
measure layer per STD-WB-MEASURE-001. Ad hoc SQL queries that
bypass the measure layer are not permitted in shipped modules.
The module registers its measures at ratification time and
adds new measures only through amendment.

-----
CATEGORY B — DATA MODEL (WHAT THE MODULE KNOWS)
-----

REQ-B1 — CANONICAL DIMENSION TABLES
The module declares its primary dimension (Dim_Employee,
Dim_Client, Dim_Project, etc.) with required fields per this
standard and module-specific fields as needed. Every
dimension record has a stable external-safe ID. Every
dimension record can be tracked bitemporally through the fact
layer.

Required fields on every primary dimension table:
  entityId               — stable external-safe ID
  companyId              — multi-tenant scoping
  active                 — boolean (current state)
  createdAt              — UTC timestamp
  updatedAt              — UTC timestamp (derived from latest
                           fact event)
  source                 — where this record originated
                           (internal / import / sync)
  externalId             — foreign system ID if applicable
                           (nullable)
  externalMetadata       — JSONB for unmodeled foreign fields
                           (nullable)
  ledger_exportable      — boolean per field map (see REQ-C3)

REQ-B2 — CATEGORY-SCOPED FACT TABLES
Per STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001, fact tables are category-scoped
(Fact_StatusChange, Fact_RoleChange, etc.) rather than
monolithic. Each fact table conforms to the shared key
contract. Cross-module queries compose via the master event
log.

REQ-B3 — CATEGORIES AS LOOKUP TABLES
Every categorical attribute (status, role, type, etc.) lives
in a Dim_* lookup table with parent/child hierarchy, flags,
effective dates, and metadata per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 6
(AllCategoriesExpand). No hardcoded enums in application
code. No PostgreSQL enum types for values that will expand.

REQ-B4 — MULTI-TENANT SCOPING
Every dimension and fact table includes companyId from day
one, even if the module ships single-tenant for DDL's own
use. Retrofitting multi-tenant scoping after a module has
production data is prohibitive. The scoping is architectural,
not feature.

-----
CATEGORY C — INTERFACE (HOW THE MODULE PRESENTS ITSELF)
-----

REQ-C1 — RELATIONALRENDERING METADATA
Per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 8, every field on every
dimension and every token/measure carries visibility and
editability metadata for each viewer-relationship class
(self, direct_manager, management_chain, backoffice,
operator, peer). Module 1 may expose limited viewer classes
in its UI, but the metadata columns exist from day one.

REQ-C2 — SCENARIO DASHBOARDS (STAGE 1)
Per CR-WB-ANALYTICS-001, the module ships with 3-5 scenario
dashboards grouped by themes that emerge from its measure
composition. Each dashboard's charts reference the measure
layer, not ad hoc SQL. Themes are determined by the data,
not by prescription.

The first dashboard must be useful immediately on module
load. Zero configuration. Customers opening the module see
value within five seconds of first view.

REQ-C3 — LEDGER-COMPATIBILITY DECLARATION
Per CR-WB-CANON-001 Candidate 10 (PortableRecord), the
module declares which of its fields are eligible for Ledger

Operator ratification per module confirms the export set.

-----
CATEGORY D — GOVERNANCE (HOW THE MODULE IS ACCOUNTABLE)
-----

REQ-D1 — MODULE MANIFEST
Every module publishes a manifest file declaring:
  - Module ID and name
  - Primary dimension table(s)
  - Category-scoped fact tables
  - Registered measures (with STD-WB-MEASURE-001 metadata)
  - Ledger-exportable fields
  - Scenario dashboard themes and chart inventory
  - Dependencies on other modules (if any)
  - Dependencies on external services (Clerk, Resend, etc.)
  - Version and changelog

The manifest is the single source of truth for what the
module is. Future automation (Dex Jr., CR tooling, integration
tooling) reads the manifest, not the codebase.

REQ-D2 — RATIFICATION BEFORE SHIP
Every module ships through a CR-WB-<MODULE>-001 ratification
review. The review confirms conformance to STD-WB-MODULE-001
and surfaces module-specific decisions (measure vocabulary,
category children, scenario dashboard themes, operator-facing
vocabulary). Modules that fail ratification do not ship.

REQ-D3 — STAGED ROLLOUT
Modules do not ship as "finished." Modules ship in stages
per the staging standard (proposed as STD-WB-MODSTAGE-001 in
CR-WB-MODBUILD-001 — CR-A). A module declares its stages at
ratification time. Stage 1 is the minimum viable shipped
module. Subsequent stages extend capability.

Staging prevents scope creep by forcing explicit articulation
of what's in each stage. Staging prevents premature
abstraction by restricting each stage to what is load-bearing
for the next.

REQ-D4 — DEFERRAL REGISTER
Every module ships with an explicit deferral register listing
capabilities intentionally excluded from the current version.
Each deferral carries a trigger condition describing when it
becomes eligible for re-scoping.

Example deferrals from Module 1 design:
  - Employee self-service UI (trigger: first customer requires it)
  - Self-scoring of tokens (trigger: self-service UI ships)
  - PII fields (trigger: compliance requirement surfaces)
  - Ledger export implementation (trigger: Ledger export
    module ships)

Deferral registers prevent the "why didn't you build X?" loop
by making the non-decision explicit.

REQ-D5 — DOCUMENTATION AS ARTIFACT
Every module ships with documentation in the form of a
Knowledge Vault wing or equivalent. Documentation includes:
  - Module overview and scope
  - Dimension and fact table schemas
  - Registered measures with descriptions
  - Scenario dashboard themes and charts
  - Deferral register
  - Changelog

Documentation is authored as part of the module, not after.
"Finished module, documentation TBD" is a failed ratification.

=====================================================================
WHAT THE STANDARD DOES NOT DO
=====================================================================

NOT — Prescribe what a module must be about
    Modules can serve HR, finance, operations, compliance,
    client management, or any other business domain. The
    standard governs structure, not subject.

NOT — Limit module count
    WorkBench can have 17 modules or 170. The standard
    scales because it is substrate-level, not feature-level.

NOT — Require every module to ship all stages
    A module's Stage 2 may never ship if the operator chooses.
    Stage 1 is the minimum; further stages are optional.

NOT — Replace module-level design judgment
    The standard is a floor, not a ceiling. Modules can
    exceed the standard in their own domain. The standard
    only enforces the minimum for substrate coherence.

NOT — Apply retroactively to pre-WorkBench products
    AuditForge was built before this standard was named.
    AuditForge does not retroactively conform to
    STD-WB-MODULE-001. If AuditForge ever becomes a WorkBench
    module (by explicit operator decision and ratification),
    it would need to conform at that point. Until then,
    AuditForge operates under AuditForge's own standards.

ONE CLOSING OBSERVATION
=====================================================================

The module standard is where WorkBench stops being a promise
and starts being a platform. The fact layer governance says
how data is shaped. The connectivity stance says how data
moves in and out. The analytics roadmap says how data becomes
insight. The module standard says how all three come together
in a shippable unit.

Every module that ships against this standard extends the
platform's value without diluting it. Every module that

## OPERATOR’S SPECIFIC QUESTIONS (1–5)

**1. Stage taxonomy: mandatory or per‑module?**

**Mandatory, but with a small core set and optional extensions.**  
The core stages (Stage 0: Schema & Substrate, Stage 1: Core Function, Stage 2: Full Feature Set) should be universal. They define the minimum arc of any module: first you build the substrate, then you ship a usable core, then you add the rest. Modules may define additional stages beyond Stage 2 (e.g., Stage 3: Advanced Analytics, Stage 4: API Export), but the core three are load‑bearing for platform coherence.

**2. Should Stage 0 ship without external users?**  
**Yes, but only for DDL’s own use and only with explicit operator approval.**  
Stage 0 is the foundation. It is not customer‑facing. The operator may approve a Stage 0 module to be used internally (e.g., to seed data, to test the fact layer) before any external user sees it. The approval must be documented and time‑boxed (e.g., 90 days). If the module does not progress to Stage 1 within that window, it must be deprecated or explicitly re‑approved.

**3. Who determines when a stage is complete?**  
**The operator, informed by the module’s ratification review.**  
The module’s `CR-WB-<MODULE>-001` ratification review includes a declaration of what “complete” means for each stage, with specific acceptance criteria (e.g., “Stage 1 complete when HR & People can add, edit, and deactivate an employee record with audit trail”). The operator signs off on the criteria at ratification time, then verifies completion before the stage ships. No automated gate; operator judgment is the control.

**4. What happens when a module stalls?**  
**The operator may pause, archive, or transfer the module.**  
A stalled module (no progress for 90 days) is flagged in the module manifest. The operator may:
- Pause it (no active work, but not deprecated)
- Archive it (move to a `/archived` folder in the repo, remove from active module list)

If Module B’s substrate requires a feature that Module A only provides in Stage 2, then Module B must wait for Module A to reach Stage 2, or Module B must implement a workaround. CONTEXT

On the evening of 2026-04-12, during the design session for
WorkBench Module 1 (HR & People), the operator named analytics
as the whole point — and then walked through what analytics
actually means at the product scope he has in mind.

The operator's initial instinct was "client-configurable
dashboards from day one — whatever they can think of." The PM
thread pushed back: configurable analytics requires a
well-shaped data model underneath, and the operator himself
needs to be in the data to know what measures matter. Starting
configurable without concrete chart-building produces broken
UIs on top of untested data models.

The conversation resolved to a three-stage roadmap:

  Stage 1 — Scenario dashboards (default, theme-grouped)
  Stage 2 — Build-your-own configurable dashboards
  Stage 3 — Natural-language interface (Claude API reasoning
            over the measure layer)

Each stage forces the next stage's foundation. Each stage is
a complete product in its own right. The roadmap is not a
feature plan; it is a staging of architectural capability.

architecture roadmap and STD-WB-MEASURE-001 as the measure
layer standard that threads through all three stages.

=====================================================================
THE THESIS
=====================================================================

Analytics in WorkBench is staged, not built all at once. Each
stage's capability is a forcing function for the next stage's
foundation. Skipping stages produces broken products. Staging
them sequentially produces compounding capability.

Stage 1 ships a small set of scenario dashboards — theme-grouped,
pre-built, operator-authored. The value of Stage 1 is not the
dashboards themselves. The value is that building them forces
the measure layer into existence with correct naming,
semantics, and performance characteristics.

Stage 2 exposes the measure layer to customers via a
configurable dashboard builder. Customers compose their own
views from the vocabulary Stage 1 curated. Scenario dashboards
become starter templates customers can duplicate and modify.

Stage 3 layers a natural-language interface on top of the
measure layer. Customers describe what they want to see in
plain language; Claude reasoning over the measure layer either
generates the dashboard directly or walks the customer to
what they need to enable.

Each stage is independently valuable. No stage is a stepping
stone that becomes obsolete. Stage 1's dashboards remain useful
when Stage 2 ships. Stage 2's configurable builder remains
useful when Stage 3 ships. The stages accumulate.

=====================================================================

The measure layer is the contract that enables Stages 2 and 3.
Stage 1 builds it implicitly. Stage 2 exposes it. Stage 3
requires it to be well-shaped enough for LLM reasoning.

Every measure in every module must declare:

-----
STD-WB-MEASURE-001 — PROPOSED REQUIREMENTS
-----

Every measure in every module must declare:

  measureId          — stable external-safe ID (MSR-###)
  name               — canonical, lowercase-with-underscores
                       (e.g., active_headcount, average_tenure_days)
  displayName        — human-readable (e.g., "Active Headcount")
  description        — plain-language explanation of what the
                       measure computes and what it excludes
  unit               — count, currency, percentage, days, hours, etc.
  aggregation        — sum, average, count, count_distinct, etc.
  dimensionScope     — which dimensions the measure can be
                       sliced by (Dim_Date, Dim_Employee,
                       Dim_Department, etc.)
  module             — which module owns this measure
  dependsOn          — other measures or fact tables this
                       measure derives from
  ledger_exportable  — boolean (per PortableRecord canon)
  llm_safe           — boolean (is this measure safe to expose
                       to natural-language interfaces?)

Naming conventions:
  - lowercase with underscores
  - verb-free when possible (count_active_employees, not
    get_count_of_active_employees)
  - domain prefix when ambiguous (hr_headcount vs crm_headcount)
  - units in the name when helpful (average_tenure_days vs
    average_tenure_months)

Semantic conventions:
  - Every measure has an explicit time grain (daily, monthly,
    quarterly, event-level)
  - Every measure declares whether it is additive, semi-additive,
    or non-additive across dimensions
  - Every measure has a defined null-handling policy

-----
WHY THE MEASURE LAYER MATTERS
-----
- Every measure declares whether it is additive, semi-additive,

-----
WHY THE MEASURE LAYER MATTERS
-----

Most SaaS analytics fail at Stage 2 or Stage 3 because the
measure layer was never formally defined. Engineers built
charts directly against SQL queries. Each chart hardcoded its
own measure logic. "Headcount" in one dashboard silently
computes differently than "headcount" in another dashboard.
When an LLM or a configurable builder tries to reason over
these inconsistencies, the product breaks.

WorkBench avoids this failure by making the measure layer
explicit, governed, and required. Every chart in every
dashboard references a measure from the measure layer. New
measures cannot be introduced ad hoc; they are defined,
reviewed, and registered.

This is the same discipline as the fact layer governance —
centralize the contract so everything downstream can rely on it.

**DOES STAGE 1 ACTUALLY FORCE THE MEASURE LAYER INTO EXISTENCE?**

Not automatically. It needs a governance mechanism the current draft does not specify.

The roadmap as written assumes that building scenario dashboards will produce measure definitions as a byproduct. In theory yes. In practice, under deadline pressure, the fastest path from "dashboard needs to ship" to "dashboard ships" is to write SQL directly against the fact tables and render a chart. The measure layer gets skipped because it's extra work. The chart works. The deadline is met. Six months later a second dashboard tries to compute the same metric and arrives at a slightly different number because the first chart's SQL was never formalized into a measure. Now headcount means two different things depending on which dashboard you're looking at.

This is the exact failure mode the review names at the end of the measure-layer section. The review correctly identifies the disease. The roadmap does not yet prescribe the medicine.

**The fix:** make measure-definition a hard gate on chart-rendering. Specifically: no chart renders unless its measure is registered in the measure layer. The rendering function signature should require a `measureId` parameter, not an arbitrary SQL query. Engineers who want to ship a chart are forced to register a measure first. Registration is cheap — a single JSON entry — but it's non-skippable. The substrate enforces the discipline, not the engineer's willpower under pressure.

CONTEXT

During the Module 1 (HR & People) design session on 2026-04-12,
the operator surfaced a concern worth naming:

  "What are the pitfalls that will make this more difficult?
  What are the common things that matter universally, what
  platforms should we research? Not just HR & People. Just
  in general so we can plan."

The observation is that WorkBench is about to enter a product
category with well-documented failure modes and mature
incumbents. Shipping modules without studying what the
incumbents got right and wrong is how platforms repeat every
prior generation's mistakes.

This review is different from the other seven reviews in this
sequence. It does not propose a standard. It does not ratify
a module. It does not name canon. It is a research intake
document — a container for seats to contribute what they know
about the industry categories WorkBench will touch, what
incumbents have already learned the hard way, and what
regulatory, operational, or architectural pitfalls WorkBench
should plan for in advance rather than stumble into.

=====================================================================
WHAT THIS REVIEW COLLECTS
=====================================================================

Three categories of input:

1. PITFALLS
   Failure modes that have bitten other modular business OSes.
   Architectural mistakes that are hard to retrofit. Regulatory
   gotchas that surprise new entrants. Operational patterns
   that look fine at small scale and break at larger scale.

2. RESEARCH TARGETS
   Specific platforms worth studying. What they got right.
   What they got wrong. What they had to retrofit. What their
   customers complain about. What their architecture reveals
   about the category.

3. STANDARDS TO STUDY
   Industry-standard practices, data models, vocabulary
   conventions, compliance frameworks. What to adopt wholesale.
   What to adapt. What to deliberately break from.

=====================================================================
OPENING SET OF PITFALLS — SURFACED BY PM THREAD
=====================================================================

PITFALL-1 — DATA RESIDENCY AND JURISDICTIONAL PRIVACY LAW
GDPR, CCPA, state-by-state US privacy laws, Canadian PIPEDA,
Brazil LGPD. Each regime has different requirements for
consent, right-to-deletion, data portability, and breach
notification. Products that ship without planning for data
residency find themselves rebuilding their data layer when
they expand to new jurisdictions. What architectural decisions
today preserve multi-jurisdictional flexibility?

PITFALL-2 — AUDIT LOG REQUIREMENTS AT COMPLIANCE SCALE
SOC 2, HIPAA-adjacent work, PCI DSS, ISO 27001. Each framework
has specific audit trail requirements. Immutable fact tables
(per STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001) are a good start, but compliance
auditors also want user-action attribution, session tracking,
admin-action escalation logs, and specific retention windows.
What does WorkBench need to capture from day one to avoid
retrofitting compliance capability later?

PITFALL-3 — SOFT DELETE VS HARD DELETE
The classic trap. Customers request deletion; regulators
require deletion; backups contain deleted records; analytics
aggregates include or exclude deleted records inconsistently;
foreign key constraints prevent deletion without cascading;
cascading deletion destroys audit trails. Every mature HRIS
and accounting platform has a deletion policy horror story.
What is WorkBench's deletion model, and at what granularity?

and accounting platform has a deletion policy horror story.
What is WorkBench's deletion model, and at what granularity?

PITFALL-4 — CURRENCY, LOCALE, AND TIMEZONE HANDLING
UTC timestamps (per STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001) address one axis.
Currency is a separate problem: multi-currency storage,
conversion rates, historical conversion (what was the rate
on the transaction date vs the reporting date), rounding
rules, display formats. Locale affects number formatting,
date formatting, name ordering. Platforms that ship US-only
and expand internationally rebuild these systems painfully.

PITFALL-5 — PERMISSION MODELS
RBAC (role-based) vs ABAC (attribute-based) vs hybrid.
Pure RBAC explodes combinatorically as roles proliferate.
Pure ABAC is flexible but slow and hard to audit. Hybrid
is the mature answer but complex to design. What permission
model does WorkBench commit to, and when does that commitment
need to be architecturally supported vs operationally deferred?

PITFALL-6 — DATA EXPORT EXPECTATIONS AT CHURN
Customers leaving the platform expect their data out.
Regulators require it. The PortableRecord canon (CR-WB-CANON-001,
Candidate 10) addresses individual entity portability, but
what about wholesale customer data export? CSV dumps?
Postgres backups? Proprietary formats? Third-party migration
tools? WorkBench's Bring Your Data stance implies a symmetric
"Take Your Data" stance on exit. What does that look like?

PITFALL-7 — MULTI-TENANT LEAK CLASSES
Every multi-tenant SaaS has at least one embarrassing story
about one customer seeing another's data. The leak classes
are well-documented: missing WHERE clauses, cached queries,
background jobs without tenant context, admin-level queries
bypassing tenant filters, shared caches, shared search
indexes, shared ML training data. What architectural
discipline catches these before they ship?
obs without tenant context, admin-level queries
bypassing tenant filters, shared caches, shared search
indexes, shared ML training data. What architectural
discipline catches these before they ship?

PITFALL-8 — WEBHOOK RELIABILITY AND ORDERING
When WorkBench accepts inbound data from Gusto or BambooHR
via webhooks (per Bring Your Data), the webhooks can arrive
out of order, duplicated, late, or missing entirely. Handling
these cases correctly is non-trivial. Idempotency keys help.
Event sourcing helps. But the operational discipline around
webhook debugging is something most platforms only learn
after multiple production incidents.

PITFALL-9 — SCHEMA MIGRATIONS AT PRODUCTION SCALE
Adding a column to a dimension table with 50M rows takes
hours and locks writes. Renaming a column is worse. Dropping
a column is a two-phase rollout. Most young SaaS products
ship freely and migrate freely until the day a migration
takes a customer offline. At what scale does WorkBench need
to adopt zero-downtime migration discipline?

PITFALL-10 — RETENTION POLICIES AGAINST IMMUTABLE LOGS
Immutable fact tables are architecturally elegant. They are
in tension with GDPR deletion rights, litigation hold orders,
and storage cost at scale. The mature answer is tombstoning
— marking records as deleted without physically removing
them — but tombstone semantics vary by regime. What does
WorkBench do when a regulator demands deletion of records
that STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001 says cannot be deleted?

PITFALL-11 — API RATE LIMITS AND ABUSE
When WorkBench exposes APIs (for integrations, for customer
scripts, for Stage 3 natural language), rate limits become
load-bearing. Without them, one customer's runaway script
degrades every customer's experience. With overly strict
limits, legitimate use cases break. Rate limiting is an
architectural decision, not a feature flag.

PITFALL-12 — SEARCH AND FULL-TEXT INDEXING AT SCALE
HRIS, CRM, accounting — all eventually need full-text search
across records. Postgres full-text works to a point. Beyond
that, customers expect ElasticSearch-quality results. The
transition is not graceful. When does WorkBench commit to a
search architecture?

   - *Why:* **GDPR deletion requests** will conflict with **immutable fact tables**.

### 1. PITFALLS (Additions & Expansions)

**PITFALL-13 — Identity Resolution & Duplicate Entity Risk**  
When ingesting from multiple sources (Gusto + BambooHR + manual entry + future CRM), the same real-world person can appear with slight variations in name, email, or externalId. Without a governed identity resolution layer from day one, WorkBench will create duplicate Dim_Employee records that fragment history and break cross-module analytics. This is non-retrofittable without painful merges. The fact layer’s immutable events make deduplication harder, not easier. Research target: how Segment and Snowflake handle identity stitching at scale.

**PITFALL-14 — Event Ordering & Idempotency at Inbound Scale**  
Webhooks and bulk imports arrive out of order, duplicated, or delayed. A status change arriving after a compensation change can produce inconsistent derived state if the measure layer does not handle ordering explicitly. Idempotency keys help, but at scale the operational burden of debugging ordering failures becomes a hidden tax. Most platforms learn this the hard way after their first production incident with a flaky source. WorkBench’s immutable fact layer is a strength here only if the master event log includes reliable sequencing metadata.

**PITFALL-15 — Measure Semantic Drift Over Time**  
A measure named “active_headcount” today may mean something subtly different six months from now as business rules evolve. Without governance on measure definitions (versioning, deprecation, migration path), Stage 3 natural-language queries become unreliable. The llm_safe flag helps, but it is not sufficient. This is Goodhart’s Law applied to analytics: once measures become targets, they drift.

**The Pitfall:** You ship Module 1 (HR). It looks great. Six months later, you ship Module 4 (CRM). But you used a different date-picker library because the old one was deprecated. Then you ship Module 7 (Accounting) and the data tables have different padding and sorting logic. 
Within two years, WorkBench doesn't feel like an OS; it feels like 17 different apps glued together by an incompetent IT department. This destroys user trust faster than downtime. 
**The Fix:** You need a single, ironclad Design System repo (`workbench-ui`). No module is allowed to declare its own CSS or import rogue component libraries. If a module needs a new UI pattern, it must be submitted to the core design system first. 

### ADD_PITFALL: The "God Object" Bottleneck

**The Pitfall:** Because of the "Everything, Everywhere" thesis, engineers start treating `Dim_Employee` or `Dim_Client` as a God Object. They start attaching 500 different columns to it because "everything connects to the employee." 
Eventually, querying the Employee table requires joining 40 different category tables, and a simple page load takes 6 seconds.
**The Fix:** Strict domain bounding. `Dim_Employee` holds identity and physics ONLY. If the CRM module wants to track "Lifetime Value," it does NOT add a column to `Dim_Employee`. It creates a `Dim_CustomerMetrics` table that foreign-keys back to the Employee. Protect the core entities from feature bloat.

### EXPAND_PITFALL: PITFALL-5 (Permission Models)

**The Depth:** Caldwell noted the RBAC vs. ABAC problem. But he missed the most toxic variant: **Hierarchical Scope Bleed.**
In HR and Accounting, permissions are almost never binary (e.g., "Can Edit Pay"). They are relational (e.g., "Can Edit Pay *only for people below them in the org chart*"). 
If you try to build relational permissions into the application logic of every single module, you will introduce a catastrophic leak. 
**The Fix:** You need a centralized `Authorization` microservice/module that computes relationships. Modules ask the Auth service: "Can User A see Field B on Entity C?" The Auth service calculates the org-chart math and returns a boolean. Never let the modules do their own permission math.

**Standard:** ISO 8601 (extended format, e.g., `2026-04-13T14:30:00Z`)  
**Why adopt:** WorkBench already stores timestamps as `TIMESTAMPTZ` (Postgres binary). For API responses, JSON serialization must use a consistent string format. ISO 8601 is the industry standard. Without it, clients will have to guess the format.

**Cross‑reference:** REQ‑5 (UTC timestamps) in STD-WB-FACTLAYER-001. This standard specifies the API wire format.

**Priority:** High. Should be in API design guidelines for Module 1.

---

## FLAG_PRIORITY — PITFALL-6 (Data Export at Churn) is higher priority than the list suggests

**Why:** The “Bring Your Data” stance implies a symmetric “Take Your Data” stance. If a customer cannot get their data out easily, they will not trust the platform to begin with. This is not just a churn mitigation — it is a **trust signal** that should be demonstrated early, possibly as a standalone feature before any module ships.

**Action:** WorkBench should publish a “data export specification” (formats, schemas, timelines) before the first customer signs up. The specification itself is a commercial asset.

---

## CROSS_REFERENCE — PITFALL-5 (Permission Models) to Operator Manifest and CR-OPERATOR-CAPACITY-001

The permission model debate (RBAC vs ABAC) has a direct parallel in the council’s behavioral governance: the operator’s manifest and the “forward motion as resting state” principle both argue for **explicit, auditable permissions** that do not rely on ad‑hoc interpretation. ABAC is flexible but harder to audit; RBAC is rigid but transparent. WorkBench should start with **RBAC with role‑scoped overrides** (a hybrid) and document every permission as a governed artifact.

**Recommendation:** Draft a `STD-WB-PERMISSION-001` early, even if the implementation is minimal in Module 1.

---

## CROSS_REFERENCE — PITFALL-10 (Retention against immutable logs) to PRO-DDL-SPIRAL-001

The tension between immutable facts and GDPR deletion requests is similar to the tension between the operator’s forward momentum and the need for a landing procedure. In both cases, the solution is **explicit, pre‑ratified exception handling**. For data retention, WorkBench should adopt a “tombstone + exclusion filter” pattern, with the tombstone itself being an immutable fact (marking the original fact as deleted without removing it). This is the data equivalent of the Spiral Protocol’s landing procedure.

CONTEXT

The process was not designed in advance. It emerged from the
practice. This review exists to make the emergent process
legible, propose its formalization as PRO-DDL-MODBUILD-001,
and surface the associated standards family that supports it.
The session that produced the process also became the
canonical example of the process — ratifying itself as the
exemplar of CathedralPlanned (CR-WB-CANON-001, Candidate 2).

THE PROCEDURE — AS OBSERVED

THE PROCEDURE — AS OBSERVED
=====================================================================
The Module 1 design session produced the following procedural
sequence. Each phase is descriptive (what happened) and
normative (what the procedure should require).
-----
PHASE 0 — TRIGGER & FRAME
-----
DESCRIPTION
The operator initiates a module-build session. No auto-triggers,
no waitlist thresholds, no scheduled cadence. The operator
decides a module is ready for design work and opens a thread
with a context drop describing:
  - What the module is
  - What exists already (from other products or past work)
  - What does not exist yet
  - What the module needs to be consistent with
The PM thread restates the frame in its own words before
asking anything. If the restatement is wrong, the conversation
catches the misalignment before any design work begins.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Every module-build session opens with operator context drop
followed by PM restatement. No design work begins until the
restatement is confirmed.
-----
PHASE 1 — ARCHITECTURAL ANCHOR DECISIONS
-----
DESCRIPTION
Before content questions, the PM thread identifies 2-4
load-bearing architectural decisions that shape everything
downstream. For HR & People, those were:
  (a) How does the token system generalize across non-audit roles?
  (b) What is the employee identity relationship with AuditForge?
  (c) What is the analytics experience?
  (d) How does the data model stage for future capability?
These are discussed one at a time, conversationally, not as a
stacked question list. Each anchor decision locks before the
next opens.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Every module-build session begins with 2-4 explicit
architectural anchor decisions, locked sequentially before
detail-level discussion begins. Stacked question lists are
prohibited in this phase.
ENT

architectural anchor decisions, locked sequentially before
detail-level discussion begins. Stacked question lists are

-----
PHASE 2 — CONVERSATIONAL DISCOVERY
-----
DESCRIPTION
With anchors locked, the thread works through domain-specific
questions conversationally:
  - PM proposes a framing
  - Operator pushes back, refines, or offers a third option
  - PM restates the refined version
  - Lock
  - Move to next topic
When operator says "what do you think?", PM proposes. When
operator has an instinct, PM stress-tests it. Hybrid or
third-way answers from the operator are taken seriously, not
deflected back to the original options.
Friction points (operator hits whack-a-mole, hesitates, says
"I don't know yet") are treated as signals the question is
wrong, not signs the operator is failing. The PM reframes or
defers.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Discovery proceeds topic-by-topic, conversationally. Operator
friction is interpreted as signal about question quality, not
operator capability. Third options from the operator get
weighed against the originals, not deflected.
-----
PHASE 3 — SCOPE GATES & STAGING
-----
DESCRIPTION
Explicit deferrals with named triggers. "Module 2 when [X]."
"Self-service wing when [Y]." "Configurable analytics when [Z]."
Every stage forces the next stage's foundation. Scenario
dashboards force the measure layer. The measure layer enables
configurable. Configurable enables natural-language. Nothing
gets built "in case we need it." Everything gets built
because the next stage requires it.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Every module declares its stages at ratification time. Each
stage is a complete shipped product. Each stage's foundation
is load-bearing for the next. Deferrals carry trigger
conditions, not just "later."
-----
PHASE 4 — DECISION LOG
-----
DESCRIPTION
At multiple points in the session, the PM thread summarizes
what has been locked.

PHASE 4 — DECISION LOG
-----
DESCRIPTION
At multiple points in the session, the PM thread summarizes
what has been locked. "Here's where we are on the locks so
far." The summary is not ceremonial — it serves as a
coherence check. If the summary surfaces a contradiction with
a prior lock, the contradiction gets resolved before
proceeding.
Decisions are boolean: locked, or open. No "tentatively
agreed." Pins for meta tasks or deferred items are surfaced
separately and held explicitly.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Periodic decision-log checkpoints during the session. Format:
"Locked so far" summary, followed by "Still open" list.
Contradictions surface at checkpoint, not later.
-----
PHASE 5 — HANDOFF TO ARCHITECTURE AND BUILD
-----
DESCRIPTION
Once enough is locked to build against, the PM thread writes
a review frame (CR-WB-<MODULE>-001) summarizing decisions and
open specifications. The review runs with council. Council
pressure-tests architectural decisions and contributes to
detail-level specifics.
Review synthesis produces a build-ready specification. The
specification hands to Claude Code for implementation. CC
reports results. Operator brings results back to PM.
NORMATIVE REQUIREMENT
Every module ships through a ratification review before build.
Review output is build-ready spec. Build output reports back
to PM for integration with next-module planning.

PHASE 6 — OBSERVATION AND ITERATION
-----
DESCRIPTION
The module-build process itself evolves. What worked in
Module 1 may not work in Module 7. Every module-build session
produces observations about the process — friction points,
question reframes, successful patterns, failed approaches.
Those observations feed back into PRO-DDL-MODBUILD-001
versioning. The procedure is itself versioned, reviewed, and
refined across modules.

Every module-build session ends with an observation log.
